Ouma Karina last survivor of an ancient tongue Nluu

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
This week 90-year-old Katrina Esau was awarded an honorary Doctorate of Literature by the University of Cape Town in recognition of her contribution to the preservation of her language, Nluu. She is the sole surviving speaker of her 25,000-year-old language. Largely an oral as opposed to written language, Nluu is extremely complex with 114 distinct sounds, including 45 clicks, 30 non-click consonants and 39 vowels. To place this in context, English, Russian and Chinese have about 50 sounds.

Summary:
As a child growing up on a farm at the edge of the Kalahari, Katrina was forced to stop speaking her language, Nluu – later in life, even her husband told her her language was ugly. But in the early 1990s, Elsie Vaalbooi, a N|uu speaker made a public radio call for other speakers of the language to come forward, attracting about 29 speakers from the Northern Cape area - today Katrina is the sole survivor.
She is determined her language and culture will not die with her- she has spent the last 20 years working with linguists who have made hours of recordings while she has painstakingly repeated each work and story she recalls. But it’s a complex language and Karina is literate and so relies on visiting academics and her granddaughter to capture the language.
She is determined her language will survive and has written a children’s book the ”Tortoise and the Ostrich” and various academics have written basic readers to teach the children in her community. But late last year a comprehensive Nluu dictionary was released – a culmination of over 25 years of work, in Nama, English and Northern Afrikaans. This has given Ouma Kartina hope that her language will survive, she herself has spent years teaching children in a school out the front of her house along with her granddaughter Claudia Snyman.
But promises are plenty and funding scare. She is not short of awards and acclaim. In 2014 she was awarded the Order of the Baobab Silver, in 2017 the Deputy Minister of Arts and Culture Rejoice Mabudafasi declared Nluu would be taught in schools up to university- in 2023 she was awarded an Honorary doctorate in Literature from the University of Cape Town for her enormous contribution to preserving her language and her culture by being awarded this honorary doctorate. 90-year-old Esau stood on the UCT stage for the entire award speech – she was an incredible presence embodying so much history.
But despite the acclaim and recognition, the State have not provided for her in any way, not even funding her school. Kartina at 90 lives in a small home in a dusty suburb of Upington along with her 26 members of her family. She is the sole breadwinner providing for them with what she earn from various academics for her expertise.
There are over 6,500 languages and dialects still spoken in the world - 25 disappear every year, and with them heritage and culture.


Extra Budget Items:
Flight are limited in an out of Upington and extremely expensive

Script: Far removed from her roots - in this impoverished home, in Upington in the Northern Cape. Her body aches - years of domestic labour which began as a child working on a farm have taken their toll.
Katrina: I looked after sheep and worked in the kitchen, crawled around on my knees washing and polishing floors with a hand brush. People had to do such heavy work. I was six years old when I started to look after sheep, six, seven, eight, till I was 11 years old.
Mac: And you were 11?
Karina: I was 11 years old, 13, 14, till I was 15, then I came back, I didn’t want to stay there anymore.
Script: First lost was her schooling, then her name when the farmer called her Geelmeid- Yellowgirl. People forgot her name was Katrina.

Script: Dr Kerry Jones is a specialist in endangered languages who started capturing the intricacies of Katrina’s dying language 8 years ago. After so much time together, theirs is a special bond.
Kerry "Some of the stories are really quite horrific. ..so you know explanations of their employers beating them for speaking the language, of policemen beating family members …………and most of it was about fear that whatever was being said wasn't being understood. And so then it would be assumed that you were skinnering or you were plotting somehow. And so it's a dominance thing that unfortunately had terrible, terrible, terrible effects on the language and for the speakers, there's huge trauma.
Script: Katrina was 15 when Nluu was silenced in her
Katrina “In those days we were still ashamed to say we were Bushmen because we were not allowed to speak our language, They said you can't speak the language, it was an ugly language, and we're not allowed to speak it.
Mac Who said that ?
Katrina “Many farmers. And when we came to the brown people, they also said: The language is not a language. It is an ugly thing. It upset me when people spoke about the language like that, that’s why we stopped speaking.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: This week 90-year-old Katrina Esau was awarded an honorary Doctorate of Literature by the University of Cape Town in recognition of her contribution to the preservation of her language, Nluu. She is the sole surviving speaker of her 25,000-year-old language. Largely an oral as opposed to written language, Nluu is extremely complex with 114 distinct sounds, including 45 clicks, 30 non-click consonants and 39 vowels. To place this in context, English, Russian and Chinese have about 50 sounds.
metadata.Summary: As a child growing up on a farm at the edge of the Kalahari, Katrina was forced to stop speaking her language, Nluu – later in life, even her husband told her her language was ugly. But in the early 1990s, Elsie Vaalbooi, a N|uu speaker made a public radio call for other speakers of the language to come forward, attracting about 29 speakers from the Northern Cape area - today Katrina is the sole survivor. She is determined her language and culture will not die with her- she has spent the last 20 years working with linguists who have made hours of recordings while she has painstakingly repeated each work and story she recalls. But it’s a complex language and Karina is literate and so relies on visiting academics and her granddaughter to capture the language. She is determined her language will survive and has written a children’s book the ”Tortoise and the Ostrich” and various academics have written basic readers to teach the children in her community. But late last year a comprehensive Nluu dictionary was released – a culmination of over 25 years of work, in Nama, English and Northern Afrikaans. This has given Ouma Kartina hope that her language will survive, she herself has spent years teaching children in a school out the front of her house along with her granddaughter Claudia Snyman. But promises are plenty and funding scare. She is not short of awards and acclaim. In 2014 she was awarded the Order of the Baobab Silver, in 2017 the Deputy Minister of Arts and Culture Rejoice Mabudafasi declared Nluu would be taught in schools up to university- in 2023 she was awarded an Honorary doctorate in Literature from the University of Cape Town for her enormous contribution to preserving her language and her culture by being awarded this honorary doctorate. 90-year-old Esau stood on the UCT stage for the entire award speech – she was an incredible presence embodying so much history. But despite the acclaim and recognition, the State have not provided for her in any way, not even funding her school. Kartina at 90 lives in a small home in a dusty suburb of Upington along with her 26 members of her family. She is the sole breadwinner providing for them with what she earn from various academics for her expertise. There are over 6,500 languages and dialects still spoken in the world - 25 disappear every year, and with them heritage and culture.
